pr_title: Fix race and deadlock in SMP context switch paths
pr_body:
Two bugs found by one exerciser in #28105 that repeatedly hammered the thread preemption paths.

The first was simple enough, some needless defensive coding (not wanting to change a preexisting switch handle) could be seen by code spinning in wait_for_switch() as a completed context switch and cause the other to start running the current thread before it had spilled its context.

The second was an even rarer (and more interesting) deadlock exposed when that was fixed, in a similar area of code.  Crazy timing (possible seemingly only under qemu) could lead to two CPUs trying to run **each other's** active threads, and spinning forever waiting for the other CPU to context switch.

Fixes #28105
pr_comments: Pushing this before I have a working twister locally.  I'm seeing some weird failures on qemu_leon3 and qemu_cortex_a53 and need to see what's actually happening in CI.

Yeah, the leon3 and a53 failures seem to be phantom and local to my installation (I ran west update, I swear!)

But the handful of remaining failures are legitimate.  The last patch in this PR breaks k_yield().  Oops.  Fix incoming.
Add the needed logic to handle yielded current when it no longer gets added to the runqueue at the yield.

For those reviewing: it's admittedly true that the final patch in this series is a little subtle.  We for sure want the bug fix in the tree, but as it's just one medium bug (that doesn't actually affect real hardware due to timing constraints with IPIs) it might be worth considering pushing this until after the release and then doing a backport.

My concern with the third commit is it has this:

    if (z_is_thread_queued(old_thread)) {
             _priq_run_add(&_kernel.ready_q.runq,
                           old_thread);
    }

which is odd because if the thread's queued like it says, why do we need to queue it again?

What I see is that `queue_thread()` will flag the thread as queued without actually queuing if SMP and thread is not the current thread. Presumably this is the situation that needs to be mitigated by the conditional `_priq_run_add()` call above.

Assessing whether each call site might flag a thread without queuing it:
* Line 318 in `next_up()` won't because it passes `_current`
* 336 `move_thread_to_end_of_prio_q()` might
* 476 in `ready_thread()` might
* 868 in `z_set_prio()` would if it isn't passed `_current`
* 1291 in `z_impl_k_thread_deadline_set()` would if it isn't passed `_current`
* 1323 in `z_impl_k_yield()` won't because it passes `_current`

At least 336 and 1291 leave me worried that a thread might be marked as queued, but never actually be queued, as I dont see a path from them to `z_requeue_current()` which is the only other place flagged-without-being-queued might be fixed.  I didn't look closely at the other potential call sites.

What prevents this from leaving a thread flagged as queued but not in a queue?

I swear I convinced myself the leon3 failures had disappeared, but they hadn't and the root cause was a broken arch_switch() on sparc.  Worked around here (it's simple), root cause bug linked.

@pabigot The point to the refactor in the second patch is to clarify that the run queue (_priq_run_add/remove()) and QUEUED flags get managed through the same API, and that they are identical exactly **except** for the case of _current, which remains outside the global run queue until the point of a context switch.  That happens in two spots: synchronously in kswap.h:do_swap() and via interrupt return where z_get_next_switch_handle() is called to fetch the next thread.
Pfft.  ARM64 had a different bug with arch_switch().  NOW it should work, heh.

Squash the bug workaround patch into the main change, as I realized (1) that this can be implemented by just disabling that write on !SMP (thus making it a performance win and not a workaround) and (2) it broke bisectability anyway.  Also rewrite the docs on arch_switch(), as they weren't great and probably part of the problem at the arch layer.

issue_context.title: sporadic "Attempt to resume un-suspended thread object" faults on x86-64
issue_context.body:
**Describe the bug**
For some time now we have seen weird behavior on x86_64 where a thread object that was not suspended was being resumed, or the same thread was being scheduled on two CPUs at the same time. A typical backtrace:

```
START - test_fs_read
E: Page fault at address 0xb9 (error code 0x10)
E: Linear address not present in page tables
E: Access violation: supervisor thread not allowed to execute
E: PTE: not present
E: RAX: 0x0000000000104522 RBX: 0x0000000000125780 RCX: 0x000000000000000c RDX: 0x0000000000000138
E: RSI: 0x000000000014e000 RDI: 0x0000000000138000 RBP: 0x000000000013a3f8 RSP: 0x0000000000140e80
E:  R8: 0x000000000014b578  R9: 0x0000000000000000 R10: 0x0000000000000000 R11: 0x0000000000000000
E: R12: 0x0000000000000000 R13: 0x000000000014b578 R14: 0x0000000000104522 R15: 0x0000000000000000
E: RSP: 0x0000000000140e80 RFLAGS: 0x0000000000000246 CS: 0x0018 CR3: 0x0000000000150000
E: RIP: 0x00000000000000b9
E: Attempt to resume un-suspended thread object
E: >>> ZEPHYR FATAL ERROR 4: Kernel panic on CPU 1
E: Current thread: 0x0000000000126220 (main)
E: Halting system
```

I have a hypothesis that this is at least in part a race condition between the determination of the next thread to run in `next_up()` and performing the actual context switch. I suspect this has to be atomic with respect to the `sched_spinlock`, as this lock's scope includes any changes in thread state.

Currently, in both x86_64's interrupt exit handling path, and the core kernel implementation of `do_swap()`, some API (either `z_get_next_switch_handle()` or `z_get_next_ready_thread()`) is called to determine the next thread to schedule, both end up invoking `next_up()`. This is then used to perform the context switch in `arch_switch()`. The `sched_spinlock` is not held in between these two events, only local CPU interrupts are disabled. The thread state could change in the meantime due to activity on some other CPU.

If this holds, I am not yet completely sure the best way to adjust the interrupt exit path on x86_64. But for the C code in `do_swap()` I had an idea we could replace this bit:

```
	if (is_spinlock) {
		k_spin_release(lock);
	}
```

with an operation to atomically re-queue whatever lock was provided, to the sched_spinlock. If the sched_spinlock was already provided, do nothing and keep it locked. If local interrupts were just locked (z_swap_irqlock() for example), just grab the sched_spinlock. Whatever the case, hold sched_spinlock through the determination of the next ready thread and the subsequent context switch call to the end of do_swap().

I expect this is also an issue on ARC HS, our other platform which supports SMP.
comments: Next step is to confirm the bug by identifying some specific thread state change scenarios across CPUs that will reproduce some of these "attempt to resume unsuspended thread object" faults. Need to make extra sure that the scheduler framework doesn't have some other way of compensating for an obsolete scheduling decision being executed, just in case I missed something.

I spoke offline with @andyross and we think the context switch in the bug description may not be a problem, but we agree that https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/28105#issuecomment-696317757 is very likely a bug. I am looking deeper at it.

I have a patch now to close the potential race when un-pending threads from IPC wait queues.
Unfortunately, these crashes are still reproducible with that applied, samples/userspace/shared_mem still eventually always crashes for me if you let it run long enough. More digging needed.

Thanks, this is interesting.  Two questions:

First, can you reproduce this on real hardware, or just qemu?  When I ran my reproducer on upsquared there were no failures.

Second,
> 2. On CPU1, a lower priority thread makes the high priority thread runnable but continues running itself
> 3. The high priority thread then preempts CPU1 and CPU0 would be expected to pick up the low priority thread

That seems like a sub-optimal solution.  Is it feasible to detect that CPU0 is idle and make it pick-up the high priority thread, instead of swapping CPUs and all related context?

I tried it briefly on my up2 and didn't see the problem, but I believe for sure this is real and not an emulator bug.  If I had to guess the effective latency for an interprocessor interrupt on qemu is much higher (it's a unix signal delivered by the host OS to a separate thread vs. a few clock cycles of transit through an interrupt controller) so gives more window for things to go wrong (which in this case means the local CPU gets preempted -- that probably happens faster on hardware and the other CPU picks up the thread before the local one can make its way to z_swap()).

As far as performance: that's going to be application dependent really.   Always running the new thread on the idle CPU gets it to run faster (except maybe on qemu, see above) and makes for better parallelism, but if it involves work with cache-resident data on the local CPU (it probably does if you just woke it up) it might actually end up doing the high priority work with lower latency even though the low priority thread sees better throughput.  Some apps are going to choose one, some the other.

In general apps with really severe requirements like that should be managing their own CPU assignments and workloads.  We have APIs for that too.  But the default seems not completely wrong.

review_comments:
>  **except** for the case of _current, which remains outside the global run queue until the point of a context switch.

A-hah.  I misread the condition.

    !IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_SMP) || th != _current;

does not mean "don't queue if SMP and *not* current thread.  It's equivalent to the **much** clearer expression:

    !(IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_SMP) && (th == _current));

which means "don't queue if SMP and *is* current thread".

Then it makes sense.

I wouldn't object to using the alternative expression here.
